title: Deliberate Practice: Why Great Teaching Isn't Built on Experience Alone
author: Dr Haili Hughes
summary: Hughes argues that teaching expertise is built through deliberate, structured practice rather than years served, drawing on Joellen Killion's work identifying deliberate practice as a defining feature of effective instructional coaching. She describes a typical coaching cycle - set a goal, observe modelling, rehearse, receive feedback, reflect, repeat - and argues coaching gives this practice its structure and precision by focusing on discrete instructional behaviours rather than vague aspirations. The piece uses the analogy of a driver with twenty years' experience who may really only have one year of experience repeated twenty times, arguing teachers risk the same stagnation without feedback loops. She highlights La Trobe University's practice labs as a concrete example of practice-based teacher education, allowing pre-service teachers to rehearse core skills before facing the full complexity of a live classroom, and closes by arguing every teacher, not just novices, can benefit from ongoing deliberate practice.
points: Hughes's central claim, drawn from Killion's research, is that deliberate practice - not experience alone - is what converts professional learning into improved classroom performance.

Her driving analogy ('twenty years of driving... often means one year of experience repeated twenty times') makes vivid the risk that unexamined repetition entrenches habits rather than building expertise.
She highlights La Trobe University's practice labs as a concrete model for rehearsing teaching skills in a low-risk setting before, during and alongside professional placements.
She extends the argument beyond novices, insisting deliberate practice - goal setting, modelling, feedback, rehearsal, reflection - remains valuable for teachers at any career stage.
quotes: A recent chapter by Joellen Killion in the Third International Handbook of Educational Change highlights deliberate practice as one of the defining features of effective instructional coaching. Alongside goal setting, modelling and feedback, deliberate practice enables teachers to translate professional learning into improved classroom practice.
Twenty years of driving does not automatically make someone an expert driver. It often means one year of experience repeated twenty times. Teaching can be similar.

La Trobe University's practice labs represent an impressive investment in this approach. They provide environments where pre-service teachers can rehearse core teaching practices before, during and alongside their professional placements.
Confidence is often assumed to emerge naturally with experience. In reality, confidence grows when people repeatedly experience success performing challenging tasks.

The same coaching cycle of goal setting, modelling, feedback, rehearsal and reflection remains valuable whether someone has taught for one year or thirty. Professional learning therefore becomes an ongoing process rather than an occasional workshop.
